q21.passage:
John was the captain of a ship and a proud member of the Marine Police Force. He had served the department with complete responsibility for eight years. He loved sailing; the smell of the sea and the freshness of the wind made him feel calm and rejuvenated. He had spent a part of his life catching criminals at sea, and pursuing them gave him strength to fight the wrongs of society.

One day, off duty, John was sailing with his friends James, Sam and David. They spent time fishing and laughing together. "John, you finally get a break from chasing criminals!" said James. "Yes, but the sea always keeps me alert," John smiled.

On their way back, in the middle of the ocean, they saw a ship releasing a huge amount of oil into the water. "They're poisoning the sea!" cried Sam. John shouted across the waves, "Stop! What you're doing is illegal!" Instead of stopping, the ship sped away. "Their ship is too fast. We'll never catch them in this boat," said David, worried. "Then we'll report them. No one escapes the Marine Police Force," said John.

At the shore John radioed the base: a ship named Molly had been releasing oil into the sea. His friends stood beside him. "Polluting the sea is a crime against nature. We support the Marine Police Force," said Sam. "Count us in, John. The ocean deserves protection," added David. The whole force searched for Molly, and after hours of pursuit it was seized. Smuggled goods were found on board: the men were polluters and smugglers too. The culprits were arrested, and John was honoured at the headquarters for his vigilance and leadership. He called it an unforgettable experience.
items: Why was John considered a proud captain in the Marine Police Force?
He had served the department responsibly for eight years, loved the sea and had spent years catching criminals at sea, fighting the wrongs of society.
What made John feel calm and rejuvenated whenever he sailed at sea?
The smell of the sea and the freshness of the wind made him feel calm and rejuvenated, as if he were on top of the world.
How did John spend his leisure time with friends while off duty?
He went sailing with his friends, fishing and laughing together, relaxing at sea.
Why did David worry about catching the polluting ship named Molly?
Molly was much faster than their small boat, so David feared they would never be able to catch it.
How did John's friends show their support for protecting the ocean?
They stood beside him at the shore, called polluting the sea a crime against nature and said they supported the Marine Police Force in stopping the polluters.

q23: Write a paragraph (150–200 words) discussing the distraction caused by the excessive use of mobile phones by children.

Mobile Phones and Children
Mobile phones have become constant companions of children today. They are useful for online classes, information and keeping in touch, but their excessive use has become a serious distraction. Many children spend hours on games, short videos and social media, and lose track of time. Studies suffer because attention keeps shifting to notifications, and homework is left half done. Late-night scrolling cuts into sleep, so children feel tired and irritable in class. Physical play and outdoor games are replaced by screens, leading to poor fitness, eye strain and bad posture. Children also talk less with their families and friends face to face, and some are exposed to unsuitable content or cyberbullying. Parents and teachers must work together: phones should be kept away during study and meal times, screen time should be limited, and children should be encouraged to take up sports, reading and hobbies. Used wisely, the mobile phone can be a good servant; used without control, it becomes a bad master.

q24.passage:
(a) You start your breakfast. Assume you are eating bread today. Ask what is the bread made of? And how? You pretty soon find out that bread is made of wheat. You ask again: "But how do we grow wheat?" Then you have to ask a farmer. He tells you how he grows wheat. But you are not satisfied. You want to know why a seed (the grain) sprouts into a small plant. This plant then grows and produces more grains on its body like a flower. We then dry this flower and thrash it to give us more grains of wheat. From one grain of wheat we got many more grains. Why? How? We get the answers to these detailed questions from the science of agriculture. In the next chapter, we will learn more about India's, agriculture.

We need water to drink, and it can come from a tank, well, river, or tap. But not all sources are safe. Water from a dirty tank may upset our stomach, so science helps us understand why. In laboratories, samples are analysed using instruments like microscopes, which reveal tiny organisms invisible to the naked eye. These organisms can harm our bodies if consumed. Science shows that boiling water kills them, making it safe to drink. Other impurities may also exist, requiring different scientific methods to remove. Thus, science ensures safe drinking water. Not everyone boils water, and some sources may naturally be pure, while some people's stomachs resist impurities. Even this variation is explained by science. What matters is the clear lesson: clean water is essential, and science provides the knowledge and methods to secure it. Through these insights, science safeguards one of our most basic human needs.

Science continues to shape modern life in ways that touch nearly every aspect of human existence. Beyond ensuring safe drinking water, it has revolutionized sanitation and hygiene. Water purification systems, chlorination, and filtration plants now provide clean water to millions, reducing the spread of diseases. In cities, sewage treatment plants prevent contamination of rivers and groundwater, safeguarding public health. From the smallest household need to global challenges, science has become the invisible force that sustains modern living, making life healthier, safer, and more convenient for mankind.

So, Science has transformed modern life in countless ways, making everyday living more efficient, healthier, and more connected. In transportation, high- speed trains, airplanes, and electric vehicles have reduced distances and made travel faster and more sustainable. In communication, mobile phones and the internet allow instant sharing of information, bridging cultures and communities across the globe. In healthcare, advanced diagnostic tools, vaccines, and surgical techniques have saved millions of lives and improved longevity. Agriculture has also benefited through mechanization, genetically improved crops, and irrigation systems that ensure food security for growing populations. Even in homes, science has simplified life with appliances, renewable energy solutions, and smart technologies that enhance comfort and safety. Entertainment, too, has been revolutionized with digital platforms, virtual reality, and streaming services that bring creativity to our fingertips. From education to industry, science continues to empower mankind, offering opportunities for progress and shaping a future that is more sustainable, inclusive, and innovative.

OR

(b) Built heritage is one of the most valuable treasures of human civilization, reflecting the creativity, skill, and achievements of societies across centuries. It includes historic buildings, monuments, sites, artefacts, and archives that embody cultural, artistic, architectural, and technological milestones. These structures and objects are not merely remnants of the past; they are living testimonies of human ingenuity and resilience. From ancient temples and forts to colonial-era buildings and modern museums, each piece of built heritage tells a story of the people who created it, their values, and their way of life.

Museums and archives preserve artefacts and documents that provide insights into history, traditions, and innovations. They allow us to study the evolution of art, science, and technology while safeguarding cultural identity. Monuments and historic sites, on the other hand, serve as symbols of collective memory and pride. They attract visitors from around the world, fostering tourism and intercultural exchange. Built heritage also plays a vital role in education, offering students and researchers tangible connections to the past.

In modern times, conservation of built heritage has become essential. Rapid urbanization, pollution, and neglect threaten these treasures. Science and technology now aid in preservation through advanced techniques like 3D scanning, digital archiving, and sustainable restoration methods. Protecting built heritage ensures that future generations can learn from and appreciate the achievements of their ancestors. Ultimately, these structures and artefacts remind us of our shared humanity, bridging the past with the present and inspiring us to build a future rooted in respect for culture and history.

Plastic was once hailed as a wonder material. It is light, cheap, strong and can be moulded into almost any shape. Today, however, the very qualities that made plastic popular have turned it into one of the world's biggest environmental problems. Because it is cheap, we use it carelessly and throw it away after a single use. Because it is durable, it does not rot; a plastic bottle may take hundreds of years to break down.

Much of this waste ends up in rivers and oceans. Sea turtles mistake floating bags for jellyfish, and seabirds feed bits of plastic to their chicks. Over time, plastic breaks into tiny pieces called microplastics, which have been found in fish, salt and even drinking water.

The solution does not lie in banning plastic altogether, for it is useful in medicine and many industries. It lies in using less of it, reusing what we can and recycling the rest. Carrying a cloth bag, refusing plastic straws and segregating waste at home may seem small steps, but when millions of people take them, the change is enormous.

q21.passage:
Meera ran a small tea stall at the bus stand of a hill town. Every morning she opened at five, when the first bus left for the plains. Students, drivers and labourers gathered around her stove, for her ginger tea was the best in town and she always had a kind word for everyone.

One monsoon night, a landslide blocked the only road. Nearly forty passengers were stranded at the bus stand, among them an old couple and a mother with a feverish baby. The nearest hotel was full. Meera did not think twice. She kept her stall open all night, boiled tea and khichdi on her single stove and refused to take money from anyone. She wrapped the baby in her own shawl and sent her son running through the rain to call the town's only doctor.

By morning the road was cleared. The passengers tried to pay her, but she laughed, "Tea tastes better when it is shared." A journalist among them wrote about her in a newspaper. A few weeks later the district administration honoured her and gave her a grant to build a small shelter at the bus stand. Meera named it 'Sabka Ghar' — everyone's home.

q23: Write an article (150–200 words) on 'The Importance of Physical Fitness for Young People'.

The Importance of Physical Fitness for Young People
In an age of screens and fast food, physical fitness has become more important than ever for young people. Regular exercise keeps the heart and lungs healthy, builds strong muscles and bones, and prevents obesity and lifestyle diseases that are now appearing even in teenagers.
Fitness is not only about the body. Exercise releases chemicals in the brain that reduce stress and improve mood, concentration and sleep — a great help during examinations. Team sports teach discipline, cooperation, leadership and the grace to accept both victory and defeat.
Yet many students spend hours sitting with books or phones. Even thirty to sixty minutes a day of brisk walking, cycling, yoga, swimming or games can make a big difference. Schools should give games periods their due, and parents should encourage outdoor play instead of screen time.
A fit body supports an alert mind. If young people make fitness a daily habit now, they will enjoy healthier, happier and more productive lives.

or: Write a speech (150–200 words) for the morning assembly on 'Save Water'.

Good morning, respected Principal, teachers and dear friends.
Today I wish to speak on a resource we take for granted — water. Though three-fourths of the earth is water, only a tiny part is fresh and fit to drink. Many cities in India already face severe shortages, and groundwater is falling every year.
Much of this crisis is caused by waste. A dripping tap can waste thousands of litres a year; running taps while brushing, washing cars with hoses and leaking pipes all add to the loss.
We can make a difference. Turn off taps when not in use and repair leaks at once. Use a bucket instead of a hose, and reuse water from washing vegetables to water plants. Harvest rainwater on rooftops and in schools.
Let us remember: we cannot make water, we can only save it. Every drop saved today is a drop for tomorrow. Thank you.

For centuries, honeybees have quietly done one of the most important jobs on our planet. As they move from flower to flower collecting nectar, they carry pollen that allows plants to produce fruits and seeds. Nearly one-third of the food we eat — apples, almonds, mustard, coffee and many vegetables — depends on such pollination.

Yet bee populations are declining in many parts of the world. Farmers spray pesticides that kill bees along with pests. Forests and wild flowering plants are cleared for buildings and single-crop farms, leaving bees with little variety of food. Climate change has made flowers bloom earlier or later than usual, so bees and blossoms no longer meet at the right time.

The good news is that ordinary people can help. Planting native flowering plants, avoiding chemical sprays in gardens and buying honey from local beekeepers all support bees. Some cities now keep beehives on rooftops. Protecting these tiny workers is not a matter of charity; it is a matter of our own survival.

q23: Write a paragraph (150–200 words) on 'The Role of Youth in Keeping Our Surroundings Clean'.

The Role of Youth in Keeping Our Surroundings Clean
Clean surroundings are the foundation of good health and a pleasant life, and young people can play a leading role in keeping them so. Youth have energy, ideas and the ability to influence others, especially on social media. They can begin at home by segregating wet and dry waste, composting kitchen waste and refusing single-use plastic. In schools and colleges they can run cleanliness drives, maintain eco-clubs and put up dustbins and posters. In their neighbourhoods they can organise weekend clean-ups of parks, lanes and water bodies, and persuade shopkeepers to use cloth or paper bags. By making short videos and street plays, they can spread awareness about the dangers of littering and open burning of garbage. Most important, young people must set an example: they should never throw waste on the roads or spit in public places. When the youth lead by example, others follow, and the dream of a clean and healthy India comes closer to reality.

or: Write a summary of the passage above (on the return of millets) in about 60 words.

Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi, once India's staple food, were pushed aside by rice and wheat after the Green Revolution but are now returning. They are highly nutritious and good for diabetics, and they grow in dry, hot areas with little water and fertiliser. The UN declared 2023 the International Year of Millets, and schemes and start-ups are promoting them.
